notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Exodus 29:1–23, compiled from the available sources. I note at the end where I was unable to find tradition-specific material due to search limits.

---

## Overview

The chapter describes the consecration (ordination) of Aaron and his sons to the priesthood. The ceremony has **five parts**: (1) Ablution (washing), (2) Investiture (clothing with the priestly garments), (3) Chrism (anointing with oil), (4) Sacrifice (sin offering, burnt offering, and ordination/peace offering), and (5) Filling the hand (placing offering portions on their hands). — Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/29.htm); Dummelow (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/exodus-29.html). The actual execution is narrated in Leviticus 8.

---

## v. 1 — The Command and the Animals

**“Now this is what you are to do to consecrate Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests: Take a young bull and two rams without blemish.”**

- **Consecrate** (Heb. *qadash*) means to set apart for holy service. The LXX uses *hagiazo*, with the same sense of separating from the profane to God. — Precept Austin (preceptaustin.org/exodus-29-commentary)
- **Young bull**: Gill, citing Kimchi, notes the rabbinic tradition that a bullock was a heifer of three years old; Maimonides says two years. It typified the strength, laboriousness, and patience of Christ. — Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/29.htm)
- **Without blemish**: “perfect” — no external defects; only such animals are worthy of sacrifice to Yahweh. This points forward to Christ’s sinless perfection (cp. Hebrews 7:26; 1 Peter 1:19). — Precept Austin; Pulpit Commentary notes Malachi 1:6–14 on the offence of offering blemished animals. — biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/29.htm
- In Leviticus 8, the three animals are named: “the bull of the sin offering,” “the ram of the burnt offering,” and “the ram of ordination” (Lev 8:2, 18, 22). — Precept Austin
- Ellicott explains that the victims were to be prepared in advance so they would be ready when the investiture and anointing were complete. — biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/29.htm

---

## v. 2 — The Unleavened Bread

**“along with unleavened bread, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil. Make them out of fine wheat flour.”**

- **Unleavened bread**: Leaven (yeast) was viewed as a species of corruption; unleavened bread was therefore required as purer. — Ellicott
- **Three kinds of bread** are specified: (i) *loaves* (larger, unleavened bread), (ii) *cakes* (*challah*, pierced cakes, mixed/poured over with oil), (iii) *wafers* (very thin biscuits), anointed with oil after baking. — Gill notes the rabbinic tradition that wafers were anointed in the shape of the Greek letter *chi* (like a cross). — Gill; Precept Austin
- **Fine wheat flour**: the finest quality, signifying that these were to be food for the priests who were being invested with a high and honourable office. — Gill
- Gill sees the unleavened bread as a type of Christ the bread of life, and the lack of leaven as picturing sincerity, simplicity, and integrity — free from the leaven of false doctrine, hypocrisy, and malice. — Gill
- Dummelow notes that oil was a common ingredient of cakes in the ancient Near East (cp. 1 Kings 17:12; Leviticus 2:5–6). — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/exodus-29.html

---

## v. 3 — The Basket

**“put them in a basket, and present them in the basket, along with the bull and the two rams.”**

- Gill sees the basket as an emblem of the Gospel and its ministration, in which Christ the bread of life is carried to His people. — Gill
- The NET Bible renders “put them in one basket and present them.” — netbible.org/bible/Exodus+29

---

## v. 4 — Washing with Water

**“Then present Aaron and his sons at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting and wash them with water.”**

- This is the **first mention of a religious ablution** in Scripture. — Ellicott
- The washing was a **symbolic action** representing the need of *inward purity* in those who approach God. — Dummelow
- Ellicott notes this is one of five symbolic acts: ablution typifies the *putting away of impurity*. — Ellicott
- The Targum of Jonathan says the washing was performed in forty seahs of living (spring) water — enough for full-body immersion. Jarchi also interprets it as dipping of the whole body. — Gill
- Gill adds that after this initial full-body washing, priests only needed to wash hands and feet for daily service (Exodus 30:18), which Jesus alludes to in John 13:10 (“he who has bathed needs only to wash his feet”). — Gill
- Dummelow connects the symbol to Christian baptism (cp. 1 Peter 3:21). — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/exodus-29.html
- Precept Austin notes three OT agents for cleansing: water, blood, and fire. The external washing was the first step; internal cleansing came through the blood sacrifices that follow. — preceptaustin.org/exodus-29-commentary
- Ellicott remarks that widespread use of ablution in other religions (Egypt, Persia, Greece, Rome) was *not* an argument against its adoption in the Mosaic system, since the Sinai legislation did not abolish natural religion but improved and expanded it. — Ellicott

---

## v. 5 — Clothing Aaron

**“Take the garments and clothe Aaron with the tunic, the robe of the ephod, the ephod itself, and the breastplate. Fasten the ephod on him with its woven waistband.”**

- Moses is to put the priestly garments on Aaron publicly. The order here reflects the actual sequence: the linen *tunic* (inner garment) first, then the *robe of the ephod* (all blue, with pomegranates and bells), then the *ephod* (a short outer garment of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen), then the *breastplate* with the Urim and Thummim. — Gill; Ellicott
- Ellicott notes that Leviticus 8:7–9 reveals the investiture actually comprised **nine acts**: tunic, under-girdle, robe of ephod, ephod, curious girdle, breastplate, Urim and Thummim placed in it, mitre, and golden plate. — Ellicott
- Gill notes that breeches (undergarments) are not mentioned — these were put on privately by Aaron beforehand. — Gill
- **“Fasten the ephod on him with its woven waistband”**: The “curious girdle” (KJV) girt all his garments tight and close. — Gill; cp. Ellicott’s “girding with the curious girdle of the ephod.”
- Peake’s Commentary: “holy persons must have holy habits” — investiture with the vestments follows the washing. — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/exodus-29.html

---

## v. 6 — The Turban and Holy Diadem

**“Put the turban on his head and attach the holy diadem to the turban.”**

- The “mitre” (KJV) was a linen wrap worn turban-style. — Gill
- The **“holy crown”** or diadem was a plate of pure gold engraved with “Holiness to the Lord,” fastened to the front of the turban with a blue lace. — Gill; Ellicott
- Ellicott observes that this resembled the diadems worn by Eastern monarchs and gave the high priest a *quasi-royal dignity*, marking him as a type of Christ in His threefold office of Prophet, Priest, and King. — Ellicott
- The Targum of Jonathan says “the holy name was engraven” on it. — Gill

---

## v. 7 — Anointing Aaron

**“Then take the anointing oil and anoint him by pouring it on his head.”**

- The anointing oil was made of principal spices: myrrh, cinnamon, calamus, cassia, and olive oil (Exodus 30:23–25). — Gill
- The oil was **poured** on his head — indicating the *freeness and abundance* of God’s grace. — Ellicott; cp. Psalm 133:2, where the oil ran down to the beard.
- Gill discusses rabbinic debate about whether the mitre was removed for the anointing or whether it was folded to expose the crown of the head. The Talmud (Zebachim 19.1) says the high priest’s hair was visible between the gold plate and the mitre. — Gill
- **Only Aaron was anointed** by pouring on the head; the sons received sprinkling of oil mixed with blood (v. 21). — Peake’s Commentary (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/exodus-29.html)
- Ellicott: as ablution typified cleansing from sin, anointing was emblematic of the *outpouring of Divine grace* — and ultimately of the Holy Spirit (cp. Zechariah 4:6; Peake). — Ellicott; Peake

---

## v. 8 — Clothing Aaron’s Sons

**“Present his sons as well and clothe them with tunics.”**

- The sons received the simpler linen tunics (*coats*), not the elaborate garments of the high priest. — Gill
- Ellicott: “coats” = tunics (see Exodus 28:40).

---

## v. 9 — Sashes, Headbands, and a Permanent Statute

**“Wrap the sashes around Aaron and his sons and tie headbands on them. The priesthood shall be theirs by a permanent statute. In this way you are to ordain Aaron and his sons.”**

- Aaron received the girdle of the ephod and the girdle of needlework; his sons received common girdles. — Gill
- **“Headbands”** or “bonnets” (KJV) — these differed from the high priest’s mitre only in the manner of rolling or wrapping. — Gill
- **“Permanent statute”**: the priesthood would descend from father to son in Aaron’s family through all generations *until the Messiah* — who would be a priest of another order, fulfilling and abolishing the Aaronic priesthood. — Gill
- **“Ordain”**: Heb. “fill the hand” — induction into office by placing insignia or sacrifice portions into the hands (see v. 24). Whedon calls it “a solemn and appropriate ordination, adapted to deepen in the minds of all the holy and responsible nature of their work.” — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-29.html
- The Douay-Rheims (Catholic) renders “After thou shalt have consecrated their hands.” — biblehub.com/catholic/exodus/29-9.htm
- Haydock’s Catholic Commentary notes that “one of the other priests had to perform the ceremony of consecration” for subsequent high priests. — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/exodus-29.html

---

## v. 10 — The Bull Presented; Laying On of Hands

**“You are to present the bull at the front of the Tent of Meeting, and Aaron and his sons are to lay their hands on its head.”**

- The bull is the one from v. 1 — the sin offering. — Ellicott
- **Laying on of hands**: a symbolic act of *identification* with the victim. By this act the offerers transferred their sins and guilt to the animal. — Ellicott (citing Leviticus 4:4, 15, 24, etc.; 16:21)
- Gill states that both Aaron and his sons placed their hands *together* (not sequentially), declaring the animal to be their vicarious sacrifice, an emblem of the imputation of sin to Christ: “the LORD has laid on Him the iniquity of us all.” — Gill
- Precept Austin likewise calls it “identification with the ram as their substitutionary sacrifice.” — preceptaustin.org/exodus-29-commentary

---

## v. 11 — Slaughtering the Bull

**“And you shall slaughter the bull before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.”**

- Moses himself acted as priest *pro tempore* — Aaron and his sons were not yet fully consecrated, so Moses performed the slaughter. — Gill
- “Before the LORD” = in the presence of Jehovah, in the court before the door leading to the Holy Place. — Gill
- Gill sees this as typifying the public manner of Christ’s suffering — in the presence of God and before the people. — Gill

---

## v. 12 — Blood on the Altar’s Horns

**“Take some of the blood of the bull and put it on the horns of the altar with your finger; then pour out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar.”**

- The **horns** of the altar were where the virtue of the altar was considered especially to reside — hence fugitives clung to them (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28). — Ellicott
- This was the standard procedure for all sin offerings: smear blood on the horns, pour the remainder at the base. — Ellicott (citing Leviticus 4:7, 18, 30, 34)
- Gill: blood was put on with the finger, not sprinkled with hyssop as in some other offerings. This figures “the blood of Christ, being effectual to the cleansing of their souls … through the application of it to them by the Spirit of God.” — Gill
- Jarchi notes there was a receptacle protruding from around the altar about a cubit from the ground where the blood was poured. — Gill
- This act also represents **sanctifying the offering place** as well as the offerer. — Precept Austin (citing Kaiser)

---

## v. 13 — Burning the Fat and Inner Parts

**“Take all the fat that covers the entrails and the lobe of the liver, and both kidneys with the fat on them, and burn them on the altar.”**

- Fat was regarded as a delicacy and burned readily; its consumption on the altar signified giving the *best* to the Lord. — Ellicott; Gill
- The **“caul above the liver”** (KJV) = the membrane covering the upper liver, sometimes called the “little omentum.” — Ellicott
- Gill notes that fat can also represent insensibility and carnal lusts; burning it on the altar may signify the mortification of inward corruptions. — Gill

---

## v. 14 — Burning Outside the Camp; a Sin Offering

**“But burn the flesh of the bull and its hide and dung outside the camp; it is a sin offering.”**

- The entire animal was too impure for any part to be suitable as food — hence it was burned *outside the camp*. This was the general rule for sin offerings (Leviticus 4:11–12, 21). — Ellicott
- **Christ as antitype**: He “suffered without the gate” (Hebrews 13:11–13), a most painful and shameful death. — Gill; Ellicott
- The NET Bible renders “It is the purification offering.”
- Dummelow notes this is the first appearance of the sin offering in the law. — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/exodus-29.html

---

## v. 15 — The First Ram; Laying On of Hands

**“Take one of the rams, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on its head.”**

- This is the ram for the **burnt offering** (see v. 18). — Precept Austin
- Again, laying on of hands signifies identification, but with a *different purpose* than the sin offering: here they claim a part in the victim’s *dedication to God*, offering *themselves* with it. — Ellicott

---

## v. 16 — Slaughter and Sprinkling the Blood

**“You are to slaughter the ram, take its blood, and sprinkle it on all sides of the altar.”**

- The Hebrew verb here means to *scatter* or *splash* (different from “sprinkle” in v. 21). — Ellicott
- Practically, the blood was cast on two corners of the altar (north-east and south-west), moistening all four sides. — Ellicott (citing Mishnah Middoth 3:2)
- Gill: the blood was not applied with the finger as with the bull, but sprinkled with a bunch of hyssop. As the deity of Christ is the altar that sanctifies every gift, this signifies that His blood has its efficacy from His deity. — Gill

---

## v. 17 — Cutting the Ram and Washing the Parts

**“Cut the ram into pieces, wash the entrails and legs, and place them with its head and other pieces.”**

- Dismemberment was the ordinary practice in many ancient cultures (Egyptian, Greek, Roman) and facilitated rapid burning. — Ellicott
- **Washing the entrails and legs** denotes the purity of Christ’s sacrifice — and that when believers offer themselves as living sacrifices, their affections should be pure and sincere. — Gill

---

## v. 18 — The Whole Burnt Offering

**“Then burn the entire ram on the altar; it is a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.”**

- A *whole* burnt offering (holocaust): everything is consumed on the altar, representing **total surrender and devotion**. — Precept Austin; Dummelow
- **“Pleasing aroma”** (or “sweet savour,” KJV): a metaphorical expression for God’s gracious acceptance; not that God literally delighted in the smell. — Ellicott; Dummelow (citing Genesis 8:21). The LXX calls it “a smell of sweet savour,” a phrase Paul applies to Christ’s sacrifice in Ephesians 5:2. — Gill
- Dummelow: the phrase “is frequently employed in connexion with sacrifices to indicate gracious acceptance on the part of God.” — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/exodus-29.html

---

## v. 19 — The Second Ram (the Ram of Ordination)

**“Take the second ram, and Aaron and his sons are to lay their hands on its head.”**

- This ram is called in Leviticus 8:22 “the ram of consecration” (lit. “of filling [the hand]”). — Ellicott; Dummelow
- This forms “by far the most peculiar part of the whole ceremony.” — Ellicott (citing Speaker’s Commentary)
- Its ritual resembles that of the **peace offering** (see Leviticus 3). — Dummelow

---

## v. 20 — Blood on Ear, Thumb, and Toe

**“Slaughter the ram, take some of its blood, and put it on the right earlobes of Aaron and his sons, on the thumbs of their right hands, and on the big toes of their right feet. Sprinkle the remaining blood on all sides of the altar.”**

- The blood was regarded as the *life* (Genesis 9:4). The life consecrated to God was given back to consecrate the priests wholly. — Ellicott
- **Right ear**: that they should be ever attentive to God’s voice. — Ellicott; Whedon; Dummelow
- **Right thumb**: that they should handle nothing but what is sanctified. — Ellicott; Whedon
- **Right big toe**: that they should walk in paths of holiness. — Ellicott; Whedon
- Whedon: “Their ears were thus consecrated to listen to the commandments of Jehovah; their hands to a faithful discharge of sacred functions, and their feet to an obedient walking in the ordinances of the house of God.” — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-29.html
- Dummelow adds that a similar ceremony was performed at the cleansing of a leper (Leviticus 14:14, 17). — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/exodus-29.html
- Gill: the blood sanctified the ear and cleansed it from sins that come by hearing; it taught the priest to listen attentively to what God would say. — Gill

---

## v. 21 — Sprinkling Blood and Oil on Aaron, His Sons, and Their Garments

**“And take some of the blood on the altar and some of the anointing oil and sprinkle it on Aaron and his garments, as well as on his sons and their garments. Then he and his garments will be consecrated, as well as his sons and their garments.”**

- **Twofold sprinkling** (blood + oil) denotes a twofold holiness: *justification* by the atoning blood of Christ, and *sanctification* by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. — Ellicott
- This sprinkling of oil and blood seems to have been the **only anointing** the sons of Aaron received (cp. Leviticus 8:30). — Ellicott; Peake
- Whedon: “The sprinkling of the blood, and also the anointing oil upon the garments of Aaron and his sons, was a like consecration of these to the holy services of the priesthood.” — studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-29.html
- Precept Austin: This symbolised “the new life of God, in which the priest was henceforth to move and have his being, in conjunction with the Spirit.” — preceptaustin.org/exodus-29-commentary (citing Fairbairn)

---

## v. 22 — The Fat Portions and Right Thigh

**“Take the fat from the ram, the fat tail, the fat covering the entrails, the lobe of the liver, both kidneys with the fat on them, and the right thigh (since this is a ram for ordination).”**

- These were the portions *commonly burnt on the altar* in peace offerings (Leviticus 3:9–11). — Ellicott
- **“Fat tail”** (or “rump,” KJV): the broad fat tail characteristic of Oriental sheep, which could weigh from six to twenty pounds. — Ellicott (citing Fellows, *Asia Minor*; Herodotus iii.113)
- **Right thigh**: normally the priest’s portion in peace offerings; here it is included with the parts to be burnt because this is a special ordination ram. — Dummelow

---

## v. 23 — One Loaf, Cake, and Wafer

**“along with one loaf of bread, one cake of bread made with oil, and one wafer from the basket of unleavened bread that is before the LORD.”**

- These formed the **meal offering** (*minchah*) that always accompanied a peace offering. — Ellicott; Dummelow
- The “basket … that is before the LORD” refers back to v. 3 — it had been presented at the Tent of Meeting. — Ellicott
- These items, together with the fat portions (v. 22), would then be placed on Aaron’s and his sons’ hands and waved before the LORD (v. 24) — the culminating act of their ordination, “filling the hand.” — Ellicott; NET Bible

---

## Tradition-Specific Perspectives

I was unable, due to search limits, to fetch detailed tradition-specific commentaries from Baptist (Spurgeon, DesiringGod, GTY), Reformed (Ligonier, Monergism, TGC), Lutheran (LCMS, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Catholic/Orthodox (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), or modern scholarly sources (bibleodyssey.org). The notes above draw from the traditional Protestant commentaries that are broadly used across traditions (Gill is Baptist; Guzik is charismatic/evangelical; Ellicott is Anglican; the Pulpit Commentary and Dummelow are broadly Protestant).

**What I was able to glean from search excerpts:**

- **Haydock’s Catholic Commentary** (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/exodus-29.html) notes on the garments: a new vesture was not made for every high priest (Calmet), and one of the other priests had to perform the ceremony of consecration for successors (Menochius). On v. 12, Haydock notes that the horns were where Aaron was ordained and where atonement “for the sins of all” was made (Calmet).
- **Catholic Douay-Rheims** (biblehub.com/catholic/exodus/29-33.htm) renders v. 33: “That it may be an atoning sacrifice, and the hands of the offerers may be sanctified. A stranger shall not eat of them, because they are holy.”
- **NET Bible** notes (netbible.org/bible/Exodus+29) render the sin offering as “purification offering” and note “consecrate” = “fill the hand.” The outline from NET divides the chapter into: Preparation (vv. 1–3), Washing (v. 4), Investiture and Anointing (vv. 5–9), Sin Offering (vv. 10–14), Burnt Offering (vv. 15–18), Installation Peace Offering (vv. 19–26, 31–34).
- **Peake’s Commentary** (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/exodus-29.html) assigns the chapter to the Priestly source (P), with vv. 21 and 38–42 as later additions, and notes that the ritual presupposes the sacrificial legislation of Leviticus 1–7 (which belongs to “an older stratum of P”).

**On denominational differences**: The main areas where Protestant traditions historically diverge on this passage relate to (i) whether the Aaronic priesthood is a type of NT church office (more sacramental traditions) or of Christ alone and the priesthood of all believers (more Reformed/Baptist); and (ii) the use of ceremonial rites in ordination. I was unable to retrieve specific statements from each tradition’s own teachers due to search limits.
